source_title: The safest way to store Bitcoin was just hacked...

claims.quote: what used to be the safest way to store Bitcoin turned out to be the fastest way to lose it
claims.claim: [A Coldcard hardware wallet] used to be the safest way to store Bitcoin and turned out to be the fastest way to lose it.
claims.basis: Rhetorical framing: 'safest' and 'fastest' are superlatives over an unstated comparison set, with no measurement that could settle them. Not a checkable factual claim.

claims.quote: it's only about half as much as they would have lost if the same thing happened a year ago
claims.claim: [Because Bitcoin's price has fallen,] the dollar value lost in the Coldcard theft is only about half what the same number of coins would have been worth a year earlier [August 2025].
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: BTC was $64,137.26 on 5 Aug 2026 against $114,128.57 one year earlier, a 43.8% year-over-year fall, so the same coin count was worth 56.2% of its year-ago value. 'About half' is a fair rounding of 56%. https://fortune.com/article/price-of-bitcoin-08-05-2026/

claims.quote: Since July 30th, attackers have drained over 1,600 Bitcoin, worth about $100 million, from over 7,000 wallets
claims.claim: Since 30 July 2026, attackers have drained over 1,600 Bitcoin, worth about $100 million, from over 7,000 Coldcard wallets.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Galaxy Research's on-chain count as of 3 Aug 2026 was 1,596 BTC from roughly 7,300 addresses across three confirmed waves plus smaller incidents; adding the fourth wave (448.7 BTC) takes the coin total past 1,800. At the 5 Aug price of ~$64,100, 1,600 BTC is ~$103M. Address counts diverge by tracker: TRM Labs and Galaxy's own wave-by-wave breakdown put the four-wave total at 5,294 addresses, so 'over 7,000' is defensible only on the Galaxy aggregate the video is echoing. https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/08/03/coldcard-wallet-losses-may-near-usd114-million-as-possible-fourth-sweep-emerges and https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/the-largest-hardware-wallet-exploit-of-2026-inside-the-usd-116-million-coldcard-hack

claims.quote: they pulled it off without any malware, phishing, or lead pipes
claims.claim: The attackers drained the Coldcard wallets without malware, phishing, or physical coercion, i.e. without ever touching the victims' devices.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Coinkite's advisory and every technical account describe an offline attack: weak seeds were regenerated from a small parameter space and the resulting keys used to spend, with no device access, no user interaction and no network path to the wallet. 'Attackers exploited those weak seeds offline by regenerating the corresponding private keys.' https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/

claims.quote: your coins are controlled by a private key, which comes from a 12-word
claims.claim: In Bitcoin, your coins are controlled by a private key that is derived from a 12-word seed phrase.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: Correct as a description of BIP-39 key derivation, but 12 words is one of several standard lengths (12, 15, 18, 21, 24) and Coldcard itself defaults to 24 words. The 12-word figure is chosen because it matches the 128-bit entropy target quoted next, not because it is the only or the device's default form. https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki

claims.quote: A properly generated seed phrase has 128 bits of entropy
claims.claim: A properly generated [12-word BIP-39] seed phrase has 128 bits of entropy.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: BIP-39 defines a 12-word mnemonic as 128 bits of entropy plus a 4-bit checksum. Coinkite's own advisory uses the same target, describing affected devices as generating 'about 72 bits of entropy rather than the expected 128 bits'. https://blog.coinkite.com/coldcard-mk3-seed-generation-warning/

claims.quote: if you try a billion guesses per second, the universe would end before you got close
claims.claim: At a billion guesses per second, brute-forcing a 128-bit seed phrase would take longer than the remaining lifetime of the universe.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: Arithmetic: 2^128 = 3.403e38; at 1e9 guesses/s that is 3.403e29 seconds = 1.08e22 years, about a trillion times the 1.38e10-year age of the universe and well past the ~1e14-year end of star formation. It is short of the ~1e100-year black-hole-evaporation horizon sometimes meant by 'the universe would end', so the figure is right and only the endpoint is loose.

claims.quote: to generate keys on a dedicated offline device with a special chip whose entire job is to harvest genuine randomness from the physical universe
claims.claim: Hardware wallets exist to generate keys on a dedicated offline device containing a chip whose job is to harvest genuine physical randomness [a hardware true random number generator].
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Coldcard's STM32 microcontroller contains a hardware TRNG, and Coinkite states the device 'was designed to rely exclusively on its hardware TRNG for seed generation, with no software fallback'. https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/

claims.quote: no device took this more seriously than Coldcard, made by Canadian company Coinkite
claims.claim: Coldcard is made by Coinkite, a Canadian company.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Coinkite Inc. is a Toronto-based company; BNN Bloomberg and CBC both covered the incident as a theft from 'devices made by [a] Canadian firm', and coldcard.com carries 'Copyright 2026 Coinkite Inc.' https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/markets/crypto/2026/08/04/hackers-drain-more-than-140m-in-bitcoin-from-devices-made-by-canadian-firm/

claims.quote: a security-obsessed air-gapped Bitcoin hardware wallet
claims.claim: Coldcard is an air-gapped Bitcoin hardware wallet.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Coldcard's product page lists 'Air-Gapped Signing' as a headline feature: 'COLDCARD never needs to touch a computer. It can work entirely from a USB power pack or AC power adapter.' Signing over microSD is the documented workflow. https://coldcard.com/

claims.quote: open source, and marketed to people
claims.claim: Coldcard is open source.
claims.label: misleading
claims.basis: Coldcard firmware moved from GPLv3 to MIT plus the Commons Clause on 18 Nov 2020, which makes it source-available, not open source: the Commons Clause FAQ states plainly 'Is this Open Source? No.' The code is publicly readable and the builds reproducible, which is why Coinkite's own marketing still says 'open source', but the license fails both the OSI definition and the FSF criteria, and the restriction on commercial reuse is exactly what commentators blamed for the thin third-party review that let this bug sit for five years. https://www.tftc.io/coldcard-source-available-license-entropy-bug-bitcoin-self-custody

claims.quote: for the last 5 years, without them knowing, the Coldcard never did
claims.claim: For the last five years, without Coinkite knowing, Coldcard devices never actually used their own hardware random number generator to produce seeds.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: The defect entered the seed-generation path in the libNgU migration of March 2021 and was disclosed on 31 July 2026, a span of about 5.4 years, and Coinkite says the hardware TRNG was bypassed by a build and link error rather than by intent. https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/

claims.quote: The Coldcard's firmware runs on MicroPython
claims.claim: Coldcard's firmware runs on MicroPython.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Coinkite's technical backgrounder describes the fallback PRNG as 'built into the MicroPython embedded Python runtime' on the device, and the firmware repository is a MicroPython port. https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/

claims.quote: which ships its own basic random number generator, which was built for simple jobs, but it's nowhere strong enough for generating keys
claims.claim: MicroPython ships its own basic random number generator, built for simple jobs and not strong enough for generating cryptographic keys.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: The generator is Yasmarang, a general-purpose software PRNG added upstream to MicroPython in May 2018 and never intended as a cryptographic source; Coinkite's write-up describes it exactly that way. https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/

claims.quote: by setting a specific flag to zero, they disabled MicroPython's generator, or at least that's what they thought
claims.claim: Coinkite believed it had disabled MicroPython's random number generator by setting a specific build flag to zero.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: The flag is MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_RNG. Coinkite: 'Setting MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_RNG=0 was intended to disable the software path', and COLDCARD's production board configuration defines it as zero because Coinkite supplies its own hardware-RNG wrapper. https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/

claims.quote: Both number generators exposed a function with the exact same name, and the crypto library would decide which one to use based on an if not defined check
claims.claim: Both random number generators exposed a function with the same name, and the crypto library selected between them with an 'if not defined' preprocessor check.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Coinkite: 'Both RNG implementations had the same function signature', so the linker resolved rng_get() to MicroPython's fallback, and the guard 'reads #ifndef MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_RNG, which tests only whether the macro exists, not whether its value is non-zero'. https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/

claims.quote: because the flag was technically defined just as a zero, the check passed
claims.claim: Because the flag was defined, with a value of zero, the 'if not defined' check passed and the wrong generator was linked in.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Same primary disclosure: the macro was defined as 0, so #ifndef did not fire and, in Coinkite's words, 'the #error did not stop the build', binding libNgU's rng_get() to Yasmarang. https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/

claims.quote: every seed phrase was generated by the basic MicroPython number generator, not Coldcard's sophisticated generator
claims.claim: Every Coldcard seed phrase [on affected firmware] was generated by the basic MicroPython generator rather than Coldcard's own hardware generator.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: True that the hardware TRNG was never reached on any affected build, but 'every seed phrase' flattens a real split: Mk2/Mk3 seeds came out at about 40 bits of effective search space, while Mk4, Mk5 and Q mixed additional entropy from their SE1 and SE2 secure elements and landed at about 72 bits. The newer devices were not purely MicroPython output. https://blog.coinkite.com/coldcard-mk3-seed-generation-warning/

claims.quote: it fakes it using the chip's serial number and a timer, both of which are deterministic
claims.claim: On bare metal, MicroPython's random number generator fakes randomness using the chip's serial number and a timer, both deterministic.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Coinkite: 'On Mk2 and Mk3, the active PRNG was seeded primarily from device and timing state.' Block's engineering analysis is more specific: Yasmarang initialises once from the STM32 32-bit unique device ID (partly exposed as the USB serial number), the SysTick timer and the RTC registers. The video omits the RTC input but names the two that dominate. https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/

claims.quote: you could just loop through all possible combinations of serial numbers and timer values, and come away with everyone's keys
claims.claim: An attacker could brute-force Coldcard seeds by looping through all possible combinations of serial numbers and timer values, recovering every affected user's keys.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: Correct in mechanism and demonstrated in practice on Mk2/Mk3, where the search space collapsed to about 40 bits and the first sweep took 41 minutes. 'Everyone's keys' overstates the reach: Mk4/Mk5/Q seeds sat at about 72 bits after secure-element mixing, which is far more expensive than an exhaustive loop over serial and timer values. https://blog.coinkite.com/coldcard-mk3-seed-generation-warning/ and https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/coldcard-hardware-wallet-flaw-linked-to.html

claims.quote: In under an hour, the first attacker drained over 1,000 Bitcoin from nearly 1,200 addresses, hitting the biggest wallets first
claims.claim: In the first wave, on 30 July 2026, an attacker drained over 1,000 Bitcoin from nearly 1,200 addresses in under an hour, taking the largest wallets first.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Wave 1 removed 1,082.65 BTC from 1,196 addresses in a 41-minute window starting about 01:10 UTC on 30 July 2026, and Chainalysis noted roughly $30 million moved in the first ten minutes alone, consistent with largest-first ordering. https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/coldcard-hardware-wallet-flaw-linked-to.html and https://genfinity.io/2026/08/04/coldcard-wallet-losses-114-million-fourth-attack-wave/

claims.quote: nearly 1,800 Bitcoin from
claims.claim: Two further attacks over the weekend [1 to 2 August 2026] pushed the running total to nearly 1,800 Bitcoin.
claims.label: misleading
claims.basis: The ~1,800 BTC figure is the four-wave total, not the post-weekend one. Waves 2 (31 Jul, 76.16 BTC) and 3 (1 Aug, 207.73 BTC) brought the three-wave total to 1,367.05 BTC on the wave-by-wave count, or 1,596 BTC on Galaxy Research's wider aggregate including smaller incidents. Only after the fourth wave's 448.7 BTC on 3 Aug does the total reach ~1,816 BTC, and the video introduces that fourth wave as a separate later event. https://genfinity.io/2026/08/04/coldcard-wallet-losses-114-million-fourth-attack-wave/

claims.quote: over 7,000 addresses
claims.claim: The Coldcard thefts [after the weekend waves] had hit over 7,000 addresses.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Galaxy Research's on-chain analysis reported as of 3 Aug 2026 that three confirmed waves plus smaller incidents had touched roughly 7,300 addresses, so the address half of this sentence is right even though the coin half (W22) is not. Wave-by-wave counts from TRM Labs are lower at 4,585 addresses for the same three waves, a real divergence between trackers. https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/08/03/coldcard-wallet-losses-may-near-usd114-million-as-possible-fourth-sweep-emerges

claims.quote: The Coinkite CEO apologized and took full accountability
claims.claim: Coinkite's CEO publicly apologized and took full accountability for the firmware bug.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: CEO Rodolfo Novak posted on 31 July 2026 that the company was 'heartbroken' and taking 'full accountability for the firmware bug', adding 'We know an apology doesn't return anyone's funds. We know we'll have to earn back our users' trust.' https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/markets/crypto/2026/08/04/hackers-drain-more-than-140m-in-bitcoin-from-devices-made-by-canadian-firm/

claims.quote: Because Bitcoin has no way to rotate a key
claims.claim: Bitcoin has no way to rotate a key, so a compromised seed can only be escaped by moving the coins to a new one in an on-chain transaction.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Structural property of the protocol: a UTXO is spendable by whoever satisfies its script, and there is no rekey operation, so remediation is a spend to an address derived from a fresh seed. This is exactly the guidance Coinkite issued, telling affected users to generate a new seed and 'move your funds now'. https://blog.coinkite.com/coldcard-mk3-seed-generation-warning/

claims.quote: every transaction waits in the public mempool until a miner includes it in a block
claims.claim: Every Bitcoin transaction waits in the public mempool until a miner includes it in a block.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: True of the normal broadcast path, but not of every transaction: submitting directly to a mining pool bypasses the public mempool entirely, which is the escape route the video itself describes two sentences later. Stated as an absolute it contradicts its own follow-up. https://bitcoin.org/en/bitcoin-core/features/

claims.quote: They can then sign their own competing transaction with the same keys and a higher fee, and miners will confirm the highest bidder first
claims.claim: An attacker holding the same keys can broadcast a competing transaction with a higher fee, and miners will confirm the higher-paying transaction first.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: This is replace-by-fee, and it is what happened: Galaxy Research noted the fourth wave's transactions signalled RBF, and that victims spotting their address in the mempool 'have minutes to broadcast a competing transaction with a higher fee and rescue the funds first'. Miners order by fee rate, so the same mechanism runs in both directions. https://genfinity.io/2026/08/04/coldcard-wallet-losses-114-million-fourth-attack-wave/

claims.quote: when a fourth attack went live on Monday morning
claims.claim: A fourth attack wave went live on Monday morning [3 August 2026].
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Galaxy Research's Alex Thorn flagged a suspected fourth wave live in the mempool on 3 August 2026, which was a Monday; it moved 448.7 BTC out of 709 addresses. https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/08/03/coldcard-wallet-losses-may-near-usd114-million-as-possible-fourth-sweep-emerges

claims.quote: the only way to win was to skip the public mempool entirely and send your rescue transaction directly to a mining pool
claims.claim: The only reliable way for a victim to beat the attacker was to skip the public mempool and submit the rescue transaction directly to a mining pool.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: Direct-to-pool submission was widely reported as the workaround that denied the attacker's bot a target to outbid, so the mechanism is right. 'The only way to win' is stronger than the record supports: Galaxy noted that because the fourth wave signalled RBF, victims who spotted their own address could also win by simply rebroadcasting at a higher fee. https://genfinity.io/2026/08/04/coldcard-wallet-losses-114-million-fourth-attack-wave/

claims.quote: to hold shipments and take the remaining inventory out to the pasture
claims.claim: Coinkite halted Coldcard shipments and destroyed the remaining inventory that had been built with the vulnerable firmware.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Coinkite shipped a fix, halted shipments when the vulnerability was confirmed, and destroyed the remaining inventory manufactured with the vulnerable firmware. https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/markets/crypto/2026/08/04/hackers-drain-more-than-140m-in-bitcoin-from-devices-made-by-canadian-firm/

claims.quote: all of this could have been avoided had they just built their product with Lovable
claims.claim: The Coldcard incident could have been avoided if Coinkite had built the product with Lovable [the video's sponsor].
claims.basis: Self-evident joke used as the sponsor segue: Lovable is a web app builder and could not have produced embedded firmware for an STM32 hardware wallet. No truth value to check.

claims.quote: I started with plan mode where Lovable mapped out the flow and let me edit the plan before writing any code
claims.claim: Lovable has a plan mode that maps out the flow and lets the user edit the plan before any code is written.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Lovable's documentation describes Plan mode (previously Chat mode) as its 'planning and reasoning mode', states 'Plans are fully editable before approval', and that 'Code changes only happen after you approve a plan and Lovable switches to Build mode'. https://docs.lovable.dev/features/plan-mode

claims.quote: it built the whole thing including auth, payments, and a managed Postgres database on Lovable Cloud
claims.claim: Lovable built the narrator's predictions-market app end to end, including authentication, payments, and a managed Postgres database on Lovable Cloud.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: The three capabilities are real and documented: Lovable Cloud provisions a managed Postgres instance with auth, and Stripe payments can be set up through chat, generating checkout and portal edge functions plus tables with row-level security. What cannot be checked is the specific app: a paid sponsor's account of his own private project, with no public artifact to inspect. https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/stripe

claims.quote: It did get stuck in a loop on a database policy bug
claims.claim: During the build, Lovable got stuck in a loop on a database policy bug and then fixed it on its own after the narrator returned to plan mode.
claims.label: unverifiable
claims.basis: A private session log belonging to a presenter who is paid to promote the product; no public record of the project or its build history exists to check. Unverifiable by construction.

claims.quote: I gave the app its own MCP server
claims.claim: The narrator gave his Lovable-built app its own MCP server, letting him pull live odds and place trades from inside Claude Code.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: The capability exists: Lovable exposes an MCP server at https://mcp.lovable.dev with OAuth, available on Pro and Business plans, and MCP clients such as Claude Code can drive a project through it. The particular app and its custom server are again a private artifact and cannot be inspected. https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/lovable-mcp-server

claims.quote: Over 50 million projects have already been built with Lovable
claims.claim: Over 50 million projects have been built with Lovable.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Lovable's own Build Economy data study, published 9 June 2026 and drawn from platform activity between January 2025 and May 2026, reports more than 50 million projects created and roughly one million new projects a week; TechCrunch reported the same figures alongside the $500M annualised revenue announcement. https://techcrunch.com/2026/06/09/lovable-says-it-has-hit-500m-in-annualized-revenue-with-1-million-new-projects-a-week/
